lesson.title: Zooming In: The Rate at a Single Instant
lesson.summary: Instantaneous rate is the reaction rate at one exact moment in time, found as the slope of the tangent line to the concentration versus time curve, the value that average rate approaches as the time interval shrinks toward zero.
lesson.body:
Average rate is honest but a little blurry: it tells you how fast a reaction ran, on average, over some window of time, but it hides whatever happened inside that window. If you want to know how fast a reaction is going at one exact instant, say at exactly t = 100 s, you need the instantaneous rate. The idea is to shrink the time interval used for the average rate calculation smaller and smaller, centered on the moment you care about, until the interval is so short that the secant line connecting its endpoints is essentially indistinguishable from the tangent line touching the concentration curve at that single point. The slope of that tangent line is the instantaneous rate.

This connects directly to the graphing skills behind average rate. On a plot of [A] versus t, the average rate over a wide interval is the slope of a line cutting across the curve. As you narrow the interval around a point of interest, that cutting line rotates and shortens until it just grazes the curve at a single point, becoming the tangent line. The slope of the tangent line is the instantaneous rate at that instant, and unlike an average rate, it requires no time interval at all, it is a property of one moment.

Returning to the hypothetical reaction A leads to products from the previous chapter, the two average rates calculated there, 1.9 x 10^-3 M/s over 0 to 100 s and 1.7 x 10^-3 M/s over 100 to 200 s, bracket the instantaneous rate at t = 100 s but are not equal to it, since t = 100 s sits at the edge of each interval rather than its center. To close in on the true instantaneous rate at t = 100 s, use a narrower interval centered on that moment: measurements show [A] = 0.8281 M at t = 90 s and [A] = 0.7921 M at t = 110 s. The average rate over this tighter, centered interval is -(0.7921 M - 0.8281 M)/(110 s - 90 s) = -(-0.0360 M)/20 s = 0.0360 M/20 s = 0.00180 M/s, or 1.8 x 10^-3 M/s.

That value, 1.8 x 10^-3 M/s, lands neatly between the two wider-interval averages (1.9 x 10^-3 and 1.7 x 10^-3 M/s) and is the instantaneous rate at t = 100 s for this data set. In practice, chemists estimate instantaneous rates experimentally either by fitting a smooth curve to concentration versus time data and reading the tangent slope graphically, or by taking measurements over the shortest practical time interval around the moment of interest, exactly the narrowing process shown here. This idea, that a rate measured over a vanishingly small interval right at the beginning of a reaction is especially useful, leads directly into the next concept: the initial rate.
